newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore Jan domestic exports flat - economists.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Jan domestic exports flat - economists.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil domestic exports for January were seen falling modestly but trending up gradually in line with a turnaround in the worldwide electronics industry, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Wednesday.
Seventeen financial institutions polled this week produced an average minus 1.0 percent year-on-year forecast in nominal terms for non-oil exports, down from December's minus 0.5 percent.
This compares with a negative 8.8 percent in November and a positive 1.1 percent in October.
Non-oil exports in December were valued at Singapore $7.46 billion (US$5.29 billion) in nominal terms.
Economists attributed lower year-on-year figures for January against a relatively high base of comparison to January 1996, rather than actually sluggish exports.
During the first quarter last year, manufacturers misjudged the market for semi-conductors and other electronic peripherals, which led to a burst of production and inventory excess, they said.
But while January export figures remain somewhat flat, the worst period for exports should be behind the market as orders from U.S. computer firms are now exceeding demand, they added.
This led the Economic Development Board (EDB) last month to predict the electronics sector would grow by 10 to 15 percent this year, compared with nine percent in 1996.
Singapore is one of the world's biggest producers of computer chips and electronic semi-conductors.

The economist said that while a recovery was underway, the immediate benefits to Asian computer and electronic component manufacturers would take some time to become evident, with the next few months likely to show similarly dull numbers.
Some predicted another four to five months of lag time before demand elsewhere filters through the supply chain to Asia.
The same Reuters poll revealed an average forecast of a rise of 2.0 percent year-on-year in January for Singapore's consumer price index (CPI) of inflation.
Retailers were seen prohibited from passing higher prices to consumers, given the recent bearish economic climate, partly spurred by a downturn in the electronics sector, economists said.
Singapore's CPI was a moderate 1.4 percent for the whole of 1996.
Four of the economists surveyed also forecast Singapore's retail sale index in December, pegging it on average at 2.9 percent.
Although December figures have not been published, the government on Tuesday said retail sales expanded by 2.7 percent in 1996 in its annual economic survey.
Figures on non-oil domestic exports were expected to be released on Thursday.
